title: Many body quantum games
speaker: Rahul Nandkishore, University of Colorado, Boulder
content: Title: Many body quantum games Abstract: I will discuss co-ordinational games played on quantum devices from the perspective of many body physics. In the first half of the talk, I will discuss how concepts from many body physics may be used to secure robust and provable quantum advantage at concrete scalable tasks on already existing quantum devices. In the second part of my talk, I will discuss how already existing quantum devices may be used to learn new things about many body quantum physicsA light lunch will be served in the Bowen

title: Fractional quantum Hall effect and interlayer correlations in trilayer electron systems
speaker: Chengyu Wang, Shayegan Group
content: Title: Fractional quantum Hall effect and interlayer correlations in trilayer electron systemsAbstract: In multilayer quantum Hall systems, the interplay between intralayer and interlayer Coulomb interactions can give rise to exotic many-body states. A well-known example is the fractional quantum Hall state (FQHS) at total filling factor v = 1/2 in bilayer systems, described by the Halperin-Laughlin Psi_331 wavefunction. While such correlated states have been extensively explored in bilayers, little is known about systems with more than two layers.
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Fractional quantum Hall effect and interlayer correlations in trilayer electron systems Abstract: In multilayer quantum Hall systems, the interplay between intralayer and interlayer Coulomb interactions can give rise to exotic many-body states. A well-known example is the fractional quantum Hall state (FQHS) at total filling factor v = 1/2 in bilayer systems, described by the Halperin-Laughlin Psi_331 wavefunction. While such correlated states have been extensively explored in bilayers, little is known about systems with more than two layers. In this talk, I will present our study of an ultrahigh-quality GaAs trilayer electron system, where we observe an unusual FQHS at total filling factor v = 5/7. The state is strongest when the side layers have a higher density than the middle layer and the interlayer separation is sufficiently small, consistent with the long-predicted trilayer generalized Halperin-Laughlin Psi_33311 state. I will discuss the fractional quantum Hall physics of this trilayer system, with particular emphasis on the interlayer-correlated 5/7 state, and conclude with an outlook on new many-body phenomena that may emerge in quantum Hall systems with three or more layers. Bio: Chengyu Wang is a postdoc in ECE, working in Prof. Mansour Shayegan’s group, where he recently completed his PhD on even-denominator fractional quantum Hall effect in GaAs 2D electron and hole systems. Lunch will be provided at 12:00 PM in EQuad J401.

title: Quantum error correction and the decoding problem
speaker: Aleksander Kubica, Yale University

title: Princeton Quantum Technology Conference 2026
content: The Princeton Quantum Technology Conference (PQTC) aims to bring together visionary speakers from disparate fields that are pushing the frontiers of quantum technology by seriously tackling challenges in quantum hardware and materials, system architecture and scaling, and error correction. The event structure will be designed to allow ample time for discussion and interaction, with the hope of catalyzing new ideas and collaborations.This event is supported by the Princeton Quantum Initiative.Event details

title: Trading coherence for randomness in quantum algorithms
speaker: Aram Harrow, MIT
content: Title: Trading coherence for randomness in quantum algorithms Abstract: The power of quantum computers comes from coherent interference between exponentially many different paths. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Trading coherence for randomness in quantum algorithms Abstract: The power of quantum computers comes from coherent interference between exponentially many different paths. This can yield dramatic speedups but is also difficult to achieve. When can we replace expensive superpositions with cheap randomness? I will describe several strategies for this goal in the context of quantum computing and quantum communication. This will lead us to faster quantum and classical simulations of molecules, quantum optimization algorithms for large data sets, and a new understanding of how entanglement can aid with distributed quantum computing.
